quote: Beweise (Franz Meyer), dass es eine Function $f(n)$ giebt, so dass jede der $\infty$ viele Limesgleichungen
english: Prove (Franz Meyer) that there is a function f(n) such that each of the infinitely many limit equations [...] is satisfied.
topic: Hilbert plans to extend the parameter-expansion method from linear to higher-degree (nonlinear) differential equations and expects algebraic singularities including branch points, with examples y''=λy² and Δu=λu². He then begins constructing a function f(n) satisfying an infinite chain of iterated-logarithm limit equations, attributed to Franz Meyer.

triage.modern_statement: The limit equations themselves are cut off in the note, so the exact statement cannot be recovered. The most likely reading is this: show that there is a function f(n) → ∞ whose growth lies beyond every member of the iterated-logarithm scale. Concretely, for every k, lim_{n→∞} f(n)/log_k(n) = 0 (f grows more slowly than every iterate log log…log n). The mirror version, where the ratio tends to ∞, would also fit. Either way, this is a case of du Bois-Reymond's theorem on scales of infinity: for any countable sequence of increasing functions there is a function that grows more slowly (or faster) than all of them. It is proved by diagonalization; an explicit modern example is the inverse of the exponential tower, log* n.
triage.answered_by: Not answered as a new problem. This kind of result was already known from Paul du Bois-Reymond's Infinitärcalcül (1870s), where he used a diagonal argument (first used in an 1875 paper) to build functions lying outside any given countable scale. G. H. Hardy gave the standard account in 'Orders of Infinity' (Cambridge Tract, 1910). Hilbert credits the problem to Franz Meyer, but I found no source showing what Meyer did with it. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: In a paper of 1875, du Bois-Reymond used the diagonalization method for the first time; it was later linked to Cantor's name.

Hardy's 'Orders of Infinity: The Infinitärcalcül of Paul du Bois-Reymond' (1910) covers scales of infinity in general and logarithmico-exponential functions, which is where results of this kind are treated.
The iterated logarithm log* n is a standard explicit function that grows more slowly than any fixed iterate of log.

triage.why: The note stops before the limit equations are written out, so I am inferring the exact form (ratio to 0 or to ∞, and on which functions) from the page topic. Every reasonable reading is a classical exercise in du Bois-Reymond's theory of orders of infinity, solved by diagonalization or by an explicit inverse-tower function. It is well understood and not an open research question. I found no source that links Franz Meyer specifically to it, so that attribution comes only from Hilbert's note.
